editorNote: This issue follows the chronological 1982 series into the week beginning September 13, with home-arcade retail trouble moving onto the front page while fall computer magazines kept pushing programming languages, graphics chips, and practical applications.
morningLine: Mattel's M-Network turns the Atari VCS aisle into a compatibility story while Chicago holds No. 1 and E.T. keeps winning weekends.

lead.headline: M-Network Trouble Hits the Atari Shelf
lead.summary: As Mattel pushed Intellivision-born games onto the Atari VCS under the M-Network label, trade reporting around the launch described retailers finding defective cartridges in the first shipment. For stores, the lesson was blunt: the hottest aisle in the shop was no longer just about titles, but returns, compatibility, and whether third-party publishers could keep quality steady on Atari's dominant console.
lead.confidence: Late-September trade report describing launch problems around the initial M-Network shipment; treated as close-period retail context for this week rather than exact-day news

computerItems.label: Magazine Rack
computerItems.headline: Compute! Keeps the Fall Programming Bench Busy
computerItems.summary: The September Compute! issue leaned hard into the practical home-computer workshop: Turtle PILOT for Apple, VIC-20 joystick instruction, Atari GTIA graphics, Commodore 64 sprite and sound coverage, and Color Computer graphics. It is exactly the kind of multi-platform reading that made a computer store feel like a night school.

computerItems.label: Atari Desk
computerItems.headline: GTIA Graphics Still Sell the Atari Pitch
computerItems.summary: Atari's 8-bit line kept getting ink for graphics capability, with GTIA articles and demonstrations giving technically curious buyers a concrete reason to look past cartridge games and ask about programming.

computerItems.label: Commodore Desk
computerItems.headline: Commodore 64 Becomes a Sound-and-Sprite Talking Point
computerItems.summary: Compute!'s Commodore 64 coverage put sprite graphics and sound synthesis in front of readers just as the machine's 64K headline was turning into a retail shorthand for the next home-computer jump.
computerItems.confidence: September 1982 Compute! coverage plus prior contemporary C64 context

computerItems.label: Office Counter
computerItems.headline: Applications Still Close the Sale
computerItems.summary: Games brought people to the counter, but a practical stack of spreadsheet, word-processing, and database programs still explained why a microcomputer belonged in a home office or small business.
computerItems.confidence: Period software context anchored to VisiCalc and WordStar source material

softwareList.name: VisiCalc
softwareList.detail: Still the clearest demonstration that a personal computer could pay for itself in business planning.

softwareList.name: WordStar
softwareList.detail: The name small offices asked about when the computer was expected to replace a typewriter rather than a joystick.

softwareList.name: Turtle PILOT
softwareList.detail: Compute!'s September issue put Turtle PILOT on the programming bench for readers interested in Logo-like educational computing.

softwareList.name: Atari Microsoft BASIC
softwareList.detail: Advertised as part of the Atari language shelf for buyers moving from packaged games to typed-in programs.

softwareList.name: Atari Macro Assembler
softwareList.detail: A more technical language option for readers beginning to think about speed, hardware, and serious development.

storeShelves.name: Space Attack
storeShelves.detail: A Mattel-to-Atari conversion that made the M-Network shelf look like more than a label experiment.

storeShelves.name: Lock 'N' Chase
storeShelves.detail: One of the Intellivision-to-VCS conversions whose tighter joystick feel made it stand out among ports.

storeShelves.name: Frogs And Flies
storeShelves.detail: The renamed Frog Bog conversion gave the new blue-label line a family-friendly cartridge entry.

storeShelves.name: Frogger
storeShelves.detail: Still an easy retail recommendation after Arcade Express treated the home translation as a serious arcade-to-living-room event.

storeShelves.name: Pitfall!
storeShelves.detail: The 1982 adventure cartridge remained a benchmark for third-party design and a useful comparison point for every new VCS release.

market.headline: Third-Party Cartridges Make Quality a Retail Issue
market.summary: The M-Network story shows how fast the VCS market had matured: rival hardware makers now wanted Atari shelf space, and stores had to think about defective batches, returns, and customer trust alongside splashy licenses.
market.confidence: Close-period trade reporting and M-Network historical context

bbsNote.headline: Modem Talk Stays Practical
bbsNote.summary: The modem crowd was still small, but the questions were practical: which terminal program, which bulletin board, which phone bill, and whether typed-in listings from magazines were worth the long evenings.
posts: Need Apple II terminal settings for local board.
Trading Atari GTIA demos on cassette.
Anyone using WordStar with a letter-quality printer?

curiosity.headline: E.T. Holds the Weekend Again
curiosity.summary: The September 17-19 domestic chart still has E.T. at No. 1, narrowly ahead of An Officer and a Gentleman, with Pink Floyd: The Wall in third.

briefs.label: Retail
briefs.headline: Blue-Label M-Network Carts Crowd the Rack
briefs.summary: Mattel's Atari-compatible line gave stores another third-party pitch, but the launch story made reliability part of the sales conversation.
briefs.confidence: Close-period trade report and M-Network context

briefs.label: Music
briefs.headline: Chicago Keeps No. 1
briefs.summary: Hard To Say I'm Sorry holds the top spot on the September 18 Hot 100, ahead of Abracadabra and Eye Of The Tiger.

briefs.label: Programming
briefs.headline: Typed-In Listings Stay on the Workbench
briefs.summary: Compute!'s September issue offers the familiar 1982 bargain: buy one magazine, spend the evening typing, debugging, and learning what the machine can really do.

worldFallback.summary: E.T., Chicago, and the crowded Atari cartridge aisle make the week feel commercial, bright, and very early-eighties.
